title: High-Rate Concatenated Quantum Error-Correcting Codes for Qudits
abstract: Qudits provide a larger local Hilbert space than qubits and have recently attracted interest as building blocks for efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). In this work, we extend many-hypercube (MHC) codes, high-rate concatenated quantum codes, from qubits to qudits of prime dimension $q$. We construct the level-2 and level-3 MHC codes with parameters $\left[\!\left[6^2,4^2,2^2\right]\!\right]_q$ and $\left[\!\left[6^3,4^3,2^3\right]\!\right]_q$, respectively, and generalize the level-by-level minimum-distance (LLMD) decoder originally proposed for the qubit MHC codes. In a qudit $X$-error model, we evaluate the code-capacity performance of the qudit MHC codes for dimensions up to $q=13$. We find that the error threshold increases monotonically with the local dimension $q$, reaching $10.0\%$ for $q=13$, nearly double the value of $5.1\%$ for qubits. Furthermore, for sufficiently large local dimensions, we observe a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases substantially faster than expected from conventional distance-based estimates. To understand the origin of the observed qudit advantage, we analyze the decoding performance in terms of the entropy of the underlying $q$-ary noise channel. This analysis reveals a competition between the increased syndrome information available at larger $q$ and the simultaneous growth of the typical physical error weight at fixed entropy. These results demonstrate that higher-dimensional quantum systems can substantially improve the performance of high-rate concatenated quantum codes and motivate further development of qudit-based FTQC architectures.
summary: This work extends high-rate concatenated quantum error-correcting codes, known as MHC codes, from qubits to qudits of prime dimension q. By analyzing the code performance in a qudit X-error model, the authors show that increasing the local dimension significantly boosts the error threshold and improves error suppression scaling. This research strongly motivates the development of qudit-based architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for efficient Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation (FTQC) by extending high-rate concatenated quantum error-correcting codes from qubits to qudits of prime dimension q.
main_result: The error threshold for these qudit codes increases monotonically with the local dimension q, reaching 10.0% for q=13 (nearly double the qubit value), and exhibits a pronounced 'waterfall regime' for large q.
method: The authors construct level-2 and level-3 Many-Hypercube (MHC) codes for qudits and generalize the level-by-level minimum-distance (LLMD) decoder for evaluation in a qudit X-error model.
model_or_system: The system involves qudits (quantum systems with dimension q) and the application of concatenated MHC codes. The analysis is performed under a qudit X-error model, focusing on prime dimensions q up to 13.
key_observables: Error threshold, logical error rate ($\epsilon_L$), code-capacity performance, and the entropy of the underlying q-ary noise channel ($H_q$).
important_parameters: Local dimension q (prime), code levels (2 and 3), and the physical error rate $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes q is a prime dimension and focuses on the X-error model; the decoding process involves computationally restricted searches to manage combinatorial complexity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the encoding process, logical gates, and show the code-capacity performance and the logical error rate dependence on the noise entropy $H_q$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the qudit framework and MHC code construction, followed by large-scale stabilizer simulations to show threshold enhancement, and concludes with an entropy analysis to explain the observed qudit advantage.
why_interesting: The demonstration of a significantly enhanced error threshold and the identification of a 'waterfall regime' using qudits provides a concrete, theoretically motivated path toward improving the fault tolerance of quantum computation architectures.
